ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: There are three concentric circles in the figure, and four complete straight lines pass through the common center, dividing the entire circular pattern into many small sectors or annular-sector pieces. Some small pieces in the figure are filled with gray shading, and some remain white. Observing the distribution of the shading, it can be seen that any shaded small piece, after rotating 180 degrees around the common center, will fall onto a white small piece with the same shape and area; conversely, any white small piece, after rotating 180 degrees, will fall onto the corresponding shaded small piece. Reasoning: Because the three concentric circles and the four straight lines passing through the center all remain unchanged when rotated 180 degrees around the center, this rotation maps the entire figure onto itself and preserves area. Also, because the shaded and non-shaded parts are in one-to-one correspondence under a half-turn rotation, each shaded piece is paired with a non-shaded part of the same area, so the total shaded area equals the total non-shaded area. Therefore, the shaded area accounts for half of the entire figure's area, namely 50%.

The four center-passing lines divide each of these circular bands into sector pieces. In each band, read the shaded angular intervals around the center: the shaded sectors together occupy exactly one sector from each opposite pair of equal-angle sectors, so their combined central angle is 180 degrees out of the full 360 degrees. Since the area of sectors in the same disk or annulus is proportional to central angle, each of the three radial bands is half shaded. Adding the three bands, the whole figure is half shaded, giving 50%.
